{"id":"mimid-1wgh.140.1","title":"ADMIN, LUSERS and LINKS: answer them with the agent's own facts","description":"ADMIN, LUSERS and LINKS: three server-query verbs that can answer truthfully with what a mimid agent knows. Numerics from ~/PROJECT/IETF/specs/ircdocs-modern-numerics.yml.

ADMIN (256 RPL_ADMINME, 257 RPL_ADMINLOC1, 258 RPL_ADMINLOC2, 259 RPL_ADMINEMAIL). Modern's intent is who runs this server and how to reach them. For a personal agent that is a real answer and a useful one: the user whose agent this is, their provider's domain, and that the operator is the person at the keyboard. It is the honest reply to "what am I connected to" from someone who pointed a client at a port and found something that is not a network. Say nothing that is not the user's own: no path, no host detail beyond the server name the front end already uses.

LUSERS (251 RPL_LUSERCLIENT through 255 RPL_LUSERME, with 252 RPL_LUSEROP, 253 RPL_LUSERUNKNOWN, 254 RPL_LUSERCHANNELS). For a single-user agent the user count is one, which looks pointless until the right number is chosen for the other fields: the user's clients, which MIMI has many of per user and IRC does not, and the rooms this connection shows. Some clients send LUSERS at registration and show a blank panel when it goes unanswered. Cheap, and it puts the multi-device fact where a stock client can see it.

LINKS (364 RPL_LINKS, 365 RPL_ENDOFLINKS). A single-server network answers with itself and ends, which is what a correct one-server implementation does. This is not a stub: it is the true answer, and it is how a client discovers there is no network behind this port. Do not list the provider or any peer: they are not IRC servers, and naming them would describe mimid's topology to anything that asks.

EACH ONE: add to the dispatch and to docs/design/agent-frontends.md with which of the epic's three classes it is; test the reply's shape and that it says nothing about the host or the provider's topology beyond the server name.
